cards.t: Epidemiology: what it is and what it is for
q: what is epidemiology
what is epidemiology used for in public health
what does epidemiology contribute to medicine
cards.x:
Epidemiology is the study of how health-related states are spread across specified groups of people and what determines them. It also means using that knowledge to control health problems. People forget that second half. It is an applied discipline, not just a descriptive one.

In public health it is used to find the agent, host and environmental factors that affect health. It also works out which causes of illness, disability and death matter most. It identifies the groups at greatest risk. And it checks whether health programs and services really improve population health. In medicine it also helps with investigating how new diseases are transmitted, finding preventable causes, and describing natural history and the biological spectrum of disease. It also helps with evaluating community interventions, setting disease control priorities, improving health services research and providing expert testimony.

cards.t: Where epidemiologic data come from
q: what are the sources of epidemiologic data
what is a disease registry good for
what does the Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance Survey measure
cards.x:
Epidemiologists draw on a handful of standard sources, and each one answers a different kind of question.

- The population census gives national, state and county counts. The Vital Statistics System records births, deaths, causes of death, marriages and divorces.
- The National Center for Health Statistics runs periodic surveys of disease and disability, such as the National Health Interview Survey and the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey.
- The disease reporting system runs through the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and state and county health departments. Reportable diseases are not just infections: one state list runs from anthrax to carbon monoxide poisoning, cancer and congenital anomalies.
- The Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance Survey is a telephone survey of risk behaviors, chronic conditions and use of preventive services.
- Disease registries are state-run and disease-specific. Because collection never stops, their value is showing trends over time.

International sources include the United Nations Demographic Yearbook and the World Health Organization's health statistics. Hospital and clinic data fill in the rest.

cards.t: Clinical epidemiology and evidence-based medicine
q: what is evidence-based medicine
how is clinical epidemiology different from evidence-based medicine
what goes into a good clinical decision
cards.x:
Clinical epidemiology uses what happens in groups of similar patients to predict what will happen to an individual patient. Strong scientific methods are what keep those predictions accurate.

Evidence-based medicine is clinical epidemiology put to work in patient care. The clinician uses judgment to decide whether the available research is valid and applicable, then applies it to decisions. Good decisions rest on three inputs: clinical expertise, external clinical evidence, and the patient's values and preferences. The aim is not just a decision but better patient care.

Good decision making also leans on history, examination and knowledge, the provider's beliefs, and the risks, benefits, effectiveness, adverse reactions and cost of any intervention. Because diagnosis depends on how accurate tests are, test properties get studied as a topic in their own right rather than assumed.

cards.t: The alternatives to evidence (eminence-based and friends)
q: what is eminence-based medicine
what are the alternatives to evidence-based practice
what is nervousness-based medicine
cards.x:
These are tongue-in-cheek names for the ways clinicians decide when they are not using evidence. Each one swaps good evidence for something else.

- Eminence-based: senior colleagues hold that their experience trumps the evidence.
- Vehemence-based: whoever is loudest and most strident wins.
- Eloquence-based (elegance-based): polished appearance and speech carry the day.
- Providence-based: the decision is left in the hands of the Almighty.
- Diffidence-based: too timid to make any decision.
- Nervousness-based: fear of litigation, which leads to over-investigation and overtreatment.
- Confidence-based: bravado.

Relying on experience alone is the eminence-based pattern that evidence-based practice was formulated against.

cards.t: The five steps of evidence-based practice (the five As)
q: what are the five As of evidence-based medicine
what does appraise mean in evidence-based practice
cards.x:
The five As are the loop a clinician runs to use evidence on a real patient.

- Ask: define the clinical question.
- Acquire: retrieve the evidence systematically.
- Appraise: judge its validity (is it true?) and its applicability (does it fit my patient?).
- Apply: change practice based on what you found.
- Assess: evaluate the outcomes on patient care.

The last step closes the loop: you check whether the change actually helped the patients it was meant for.

cards.t: Purposes of research and primary versus secondary research
q: what are the purposes of research
what is the difference between primary and secondary research
is a systematic review primary research
cards.x:
Research can aim at three things. Exploration is for a new or understudied topic: satisfy curiosity, test whether a more careful study is feasible, and develop its methods. Description is careful, deliberate observation and a write-up of what is found, such as disease rates or the demographics of those affected. Explanation tries to answer why.

It also matters where the data come from. Primary research uses data the researcher collects personally, through questionnaires, surveys, clinical measurements or laboratory results, as in original research articles. Secondary research analyzes data that already exist, which is what a meta-analysis or a systematic review does. A quick test: did the authors collect the data themselves, or did they analyze what other people collected?

cards.t: Independent, dependent and extraneous variables; population versus sample
q: what is an independent variable
what is a dependent variable
what is a covariate
what is the difference between a population and a sample
cards.x:
Think of a study as asking whether a possible cause changes a possible effect. The independent variable is the possible cause. The dependent variable is the possible effect. An extraneous variable, also called a covariate, is something else that may affect the relationship between the two.

Separately, the population is all the people in a defined setting or with defined features. The sample is the subset of them who are actually studied. Nearly every study measures a sample and then tries to say something about the population.

cards.t: Bias: what it is and where it comes from
q: what is bias in research
at what stage can bias enter a study
does potential for bias mean the study is biased
cards.x:
Bias is systematic error that makes a study's conclusions differ from the true results. It can enter at any stage: conception and design, data collection, data analysis, or data interpretation.

Having the potential for bias does not mean bias is actually present. But you should always consider it, and it is often detectable when you read the article. The main types are selection, measurement, confounding, procedural, attrition, non-response, performance, reporting, publication, and conflict of interest. Selection bias is best considered at study design, and confounding at data analysis.

cards.t: Selection (sampling) bias
q: what is selection bias
how does selection bias happen
why does it matter if the groups differ at the start
cards.x:
Selection bias means the groups being compared differ in more ways than the one the study is about, and those extra differences also affect the outcome. The groups were not comparable to begin with, so any difference at the end could come from who got into each group rather than from the exposure or treatment.

Example: in a surgery-versus-medical-therapy comparison, the surgical group is healthy enough to tolerate surgery while the medical group carries more other illnesses. Another: patients admitted by doctors in different neighborhoods likely differ in socioeconomic and other traits linked to health. It is something to consider at the design stage. Also note that if two groups exercised the same amount, exercise cannot explain a difference between them, but selection differences or differences in how outcomes were detected can.

cards.t: Measurement bias and recall bias
q: what is measurement bias
what is recall bias
is recall bias a type of measurement bias
cards.x:
Measurement bias happens when the method of measurement gives incorrect results, typically because information was not obtained the same way in both groups. Blood pressure taken without a standard procedure each time is one example. Another is clinicians who question and record contraceptive use more carefully in women who have the disease than in women who do not.

It also happens when one group's outcomes are more likely to be detected. If all the surgically treated patients but only some of the medically treated patients stay under care, pain is measured more completely in one group than the other.

Recall bias is a kind of measurement bias. People with an illness remember or report earlier exposures differently because they suspect those exposures caused their illness.

cards.t: Procedural, attrition, non-response and performance bias
q: what is performance bias
what is attrition effect
what is non-response bias
what does blinding protect against
cards.x:
These four are easy to mix up, so tie each to what goes wrong.

- Procedural: the way a questionnaire or interview is delivered changes the answers, such as giving a questionnaire while the patient is still under the after-effects of anesthesia.
- Attrition: participants drop out, which reduces sample size.
- Non-response: the people who respond differ from those who do not, so the results may not reflect the whole population.
- Performance: care differs between groups in ways other than the topic of interest. For example, the control group knows it is on placebo and seeks other treatment. Blinding the participants protects against it.

cards.t: Publication bias, reporting bias and conflict of interest
q: what is publication bias
why are negative studies less likely to be published
what is reporting bias
cards.x:
Publication bias means research without statistically significant results is less likely to be published. Two forces cause it: journal editors' preferences, and sponsors, such as a company with a product to sell, who are less likely to support research that is unfavorable to it. The published literature then leaves out the studies that found nothing, and looks more convincing than the full body of research would.

Reporting bias is related: only a subset of the relevant data is made available, so the study appears but not everything it found does.

Conflict of interest is when financial or personal considerations affect objectivity. The effect may be conscious or unconscious, and authors should disclose it.

cards.t: Chance versus bias
q: what is chance in research
how can I tell bias from chance
can statistics fix a badly designed study
cards.x:
Chance is random variation that makes conclusions differ from the true results. Statistics can estimate how much it matters, and good design reduces it. But nothing eliminates it, and it can coexist with bias. Small numbers of participants make it more likely that chance explains a difference between groups.

The way to tell chance from bias: random variation is equally likely to land above or below the truth. So if a series of blood pressure readings all fall above the true value, that points to bias, not chance.

Statistics cannot rescue a bad design. Analysis can estimate the effect of chance, but no analysis can correct for unknown biases. Applying statistics to poorly designed research just gives it a false sense of respectability.

cards.t: Internal versus external validity
q: what is the difference between internal and external validity
what is generalizability
does a correct sample guarantee external validity
cards.x:
Ask two questions of any study. First: are the conclusions valid for the people in the sample? That is internal validity, the degree to which the results are correct for the sample studied. Second: does the sample represent my patients? That is external validity (generalizability), the degree to which the results are also true in other clinical settings and patients.

External validity is rarely settled by a single study. Results from men may not apply to a woman. Applying results from younger patients to an older patient is a judgment call, based on whatever is known about whether older patients respond the same way. Even a correctly drawn sample can misrepresent its population by chance, especially when it is small. So correct sampling does not guarantee external validity.

cards.t: Evidence-based medicine: origin and definition
q: where did evidence-based medicine come from
how is evidence-based medicine defined
what did Archie Cochrane contribute
cards.x:
Evidence-based medicine began at McMaster University in the 1970s. David Sackett's work gave it its core concepts and definition. Archie Cochrane pushed randomized controlled trials and systematic reviews as the tools for checking that treatments really work.

The 1996 definition: it is the conscientious, explicit and judicious use of current best evidence in making decisions about the care of individual patients. That means combining individual clinical expertise with the best available external evidence from systematic research. Evidence-based practice also takes in the individual patient's situation and preferences.

The question behind all of it is simple: how do you know that what you do, and how you do it, really works?

cards.t: Challenges of practicing evidence-based medicine
q: what are the challenges to evidence-based medicine
why isn't more evidence enough
cards.x:
Doing evidence-based medicine well is hard for practical reasons. Searching for and finding the best evidence takes time. The evidence may not exist, or it may conflict with other evidence, or it may be outdated. And findings are often written in language clinicians have trouble understanding.

Sheer volume does not fix this. With more than two million studies, thirty thousand journals and over nineteen million citations, the answers are still incomplete. More publications are not the same as the right answer for your patient's question.

cards.t: Descriptive, assessment and treatment evidence
q: what are the three types of evidence
what is assessment evidence
cards.x:
Sort evidence by the question it answers.

- Descriptive evidence: what are the features of patients with a specific diagnosis?
- Assessment evidence: which tests are most effective at identifying or predicting a diagnosis?
- Treatment evidence: which treatments work best against a given diagnosis in a given population?

Assessment evidence sits in the middle. Descriptive evidence tells you what patients with the condition are like. Assessment evidence tells you how to find or predict the diagnosis. Treatment evidence tells you what works against it.

cards.t: The evidence hierarchy (clinical studies pyramid)
q: what is the evidence hierarchy
which study design gives the strongest evidence
where do case reports sit in the pyramid
cards.x:
The evidence hierarchy, usually drawn as a pyramid, ranks study designs by how well they resist bias. Higher levels are least vulnerable to bias and more generalizable. Their outcomes are more likely due to the thing being studied.

One version of the pyramid includes laboratory work. From the bottom up it runs: in vitro (test tube) research, animal research, ideas, editorials and opinions, case reports, case series, case-control studies, cohort studies, and randomized controlled double-blind studies. At the top are systematic reviews and meta-analysis. Cohort studies sit just below randomized trials. In the clinical-only version, background information and expert opinion form the base.

A good systematic review is the highest level of evidence. A single recent article taken out of context with the other studies on the same question is of marginal value, unless it is much stronger than everything before it.

cards.t: Filtered versus unfiltered evidence
q: what does filtered mean in the evidence pyramid
are randomized trials filtered
what is an article synopsis
cards.x:
Filtered means someone has already appraised the primary studies for you. Systematic reviews, critically appraised topics (evidence syntheses and guidelines) and critically appraised individual articles (article synopses) are all filtered.

Randomized trials, cohort studies and case-control studies are unfiltered. They are sound designs, but the appraisal is still yours to do.

That is why a critically appraised individual article sits above randomized trials in this version of the pyramid: the appraisal has already been done. It still sits below critically appraised topics and systematic reviews.

cards.t: USPSTF levels of certainty (high, moderate, low)
q: what does certainty mean for the Preventive Services Task Force
what is the difference between moderate and low certainty
cards.x:
The U.S. Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF) rates its certainty, meaning how likely it is that its judgment of net benefit is correct. Net benefit is the benefit minus the harm of a service as it would be delivered in a general primary care population.

- High: consistent results from well-designed, well-conducted studies in representative primary care populations. Future studies are unlikely to change the conclusion strongly.
- Moderate: the evidence is enough to determine the effects, but confidence is limited. Limits include the number, size or quality of studies, and inconsistency. Others are limited generalizability and gaps in the chain of evidence. The magnitude or direction could change.
- Low: the evidence is insufficient to assess effects. The reasons are too few or small studies, important design flaws, inconsistency, gaps, findings that do not generalize, or missing information on important outcomes. More information may allow an estimate.

cards.t: USPSTF grades A, B, C, D and I
q: what do the USPSTF grades mean
what is the difference between grade D and grade I
what does grade C mean
cards.x:
Each grade pairs a level of certainty with a size of net benefit and tells you what to do.

- A: high certainty the net benefit is substantial. Offer or provide the service.
- B: high certainty of moderate benefit, or moderate certainty of moderate-to-substantial benefit. Also offer or provide it.
- C: at least moderate certainty that the net benefit is small. Offer selectively, by professional judgment and patient preference.
- D: moderate or high certainty of no net benefit, or harms outweigh benefits. Discourage the service.
- I: the evidence is lacking, poor quality or conflicting. Read the clinical considerations, and if the service is offered the patient should understand the uncertainty.

The trap is D versus I. D is a positive finding against the service. I is the absence of any finding either way: the balance of benefits and harms cannot be determined. It does not mean the balance is unfavorable.

cards.t: Systematic review versus meta-analysis
q: what is the difference between a systematic review and a meta-analysis
why do meta-analyses have more power
can a meta-analysis fix poor studies
cards.x:
A systematic review systematically identifies and evaluates multiple studies to answer a specific, focused question. A meta-analysis goes a step further: it statistically pools the data from those studies, so the combination works like one larger study with more power. The review finds and appraises the studies; the meta-analysis combines their data.

A greater number of participants usually means greater power, which is the appeal of pooling. But pooling poor studies just produces a larger poor study, not a reliable answer.

cards.t: Judging sources of medical information (ABCD method)
q: how do I judge a website for medical information
what does ABCD stand for
are pharmaceutical representatives a good source
cards.x:
Information reaches clinicians through many channels of unequal quality, from original research journals and evidence-based databases through experts and guidelines to newsletters, pharmaceutical representatives, media and patients. Being on the list is not an endorsement. Quality markers are peer review and government databases, and you should be cautious of websites, which carry no equivalent guarantee of scrutiny.

For a web resource, the ABCD (author, bias, content, date) method asks, in order:
- Author: credentials, qualifications, expertise in the field?
- Bias: is there any?
- Content: how detailed is it?
- Date: is it still current?

It moves from who wrote it, to why, to what, to when. Fame alone is the least reassuring sign, because a well-known expert may still be biased. Look instead for the sponsoring organization, facts and stated sources.

cards.t: The retracted vaccine and autism study: why appraisal still matters
q: what is the lesson of the retracted vaccine and autism study
can I trust a study because it is in a major journal
cards.x:
A vaccine and autism study was published in a major journal and later retracted. It shows that a respected journal and peer review do not guarantee integrity.

The problems were serious. The author failed to declare a payment of 55,000 pounds to advise lawyers representing parents. He failed to disclose a patent for a competing vaccine, and he planned to market an experimental product. He also obtained blood from children at his son's birthday party for 5 pounds each. And he subjected autistic children to colonoscopy and lumbar puncture without research review board approval.

The lesson is to keep appraising the author, the interests behind the work and the methods, even when the source looks prestigious.

cards.t: Databases for finding evidence (Cochrane, MEDLINE, PubMed and others)
q: what is the Cochrane Library
what is the difference between MEDLINE and the Cochrane Database
which database should I use to find original articles
cards.x:
Different databases do different jobs.

- Cochrane Library (Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews): systematic reviews, so the source for literature reviews.
- MEDLINE and PubMed, from the US National Library of Medicine: original articles.
- UpToDate, TripPro and ClinicalKey: point-of-care and search resources.
- Essential Evidence Plus: incorporates InfoPOEMS and InfoRetriever.
- The American College of Physicians (ACP) Journal Club: many specialty journal clubs exist.
- Evidence Based Medicine Reviews: seven leading evidence-based medicine resources plus MEDLINE and more than 200 full-text journals.

Guidelines come from the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality (which links to the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF)), the Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report recommendations and reports (public health policies for prevention and treatment), and the Task Force on Community Preventive Services.

cards.t: Searching MEDLINE: strengths and limits
q: what are the limitations of MEDLINE
when should I use MEDLINE
can MEDLINE be searched by methods terms
cards.x:
MEDLINE can be searched by content terms and by methods terms at the same time, for example the topic plus the study design. That helps narrow a search. Its limits are that it misses some articles, does not cover every journal in the world, and is affected by publication bias.

It is indispensable for finding out whether a rare event has been reported. But for most questions at the point of care it is too inefficient. The National Library of Medicine and university libraries offer search tutorials. Searching for the best evidence is itself one of the named challenges of evidence-based practice.

cards.t: Practice guidelines and who produces them
q: where do practice guidelines come from
who writes practice guidelines
cards.x:
Practice guidelines are recommendations for care. They are produced at several levels: by a hospital or clinic, nationally, and by professional bodies. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention is a national example, and the American Academy of Pediatrics is a professional one.

Useful starting points for guidelines are:
- the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality (which links to the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF))
- the Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report recommendations and reports, which cover public health policies for prevention and treatment
- the Task Force on Community Preventive Services

cards.t: Joint decision making and the steps of evidence-based practice
q: what are the elements of joint decision making
why is validity assessed before applying research
cards.x:
Joint clinical decision making has three primary elements, in order: disclosure of the risks and benefits of the treatment alternatives, exploration of the patient's values about the therapy and its possible outcomes, and then the actual decision.

Evidence-based practice runs in five steps: create a focused clinical question; do a systematic review of the literature, or find an evidence-based synopsis from a credible resource; evaluate the validity (truth) of the research; apply it to individual patient encounters; and evaluate performance or outcome. The validity step comes before application on purpose: research whose truth has not been established should not be carried into a patient encounter.

cards.t: Qualitative versus quantitative research paradigms
q: what is the difference between qualitative and quantitative research
what is qualitative research
what are examples of qualitative designs
cards.x:
The two research paradigms differ in how they approach a question and what they produce.

- Qualitative research is naturalistic and inductive and develops descriptions. Its data are observation, field notes and audio material, coming from both researchers and participants. Examples are the case study, biography, ethnography and phenomenology.
- Quantitative research is positivistic and deductive and develops predictions. Its data are numerical, objective and measurable. Examples are randomized controlled trials, cohort studies and case-control studies.

A quick way to sort them: if the data are words, observations and field notes that build up into a description, it is qualitative. If the data are numbers used to test a prediction, it is quantitative.

cards.t: What study design is and why it matters
q: what is study design
why does study design matter
cards.x:
Study design is the organization and plan for collecting and analyzing data. It is directly tied to how valid and reliable the data are: a strong design gives strong data, and strong data give valid, reliable results and conclusions.

That is why you need to know the strengths and limits of each design. It is what lets you evaluate evidence, and that makes your clinical decisions better informed. Careful analysis cannot rescue data gathered under a weak design.

cards.t: Descriptive versus analytic, experimental versus observational
q: what is the difference between descriptive and analytic studies
what is the difference between experimental and observational
is a cohort study observational or experimental
cards.x:
Every study design can be classified on two axes: its purpose, and who controls the exposure.

Purpose: a descriptive study describes the features of a group of people (case report, case series). An analytic study compares two or more groups so you can draw an inference about a population (randomized controlled trial, cohort, case-control). A case series, for example, reports on a group of patients such as those with an uncommon disease seen at a referral center, with no comparison group.

Control: in an experimental study the investigator assigns and manipulates the intervention, which is the independent variable (randomized controlled trial). In an observational study the exposure is observed, not assigned, because it happened independently (cohort, case-control).

Cross-sectional appears under both descriptive and analytic, and is always observational.

cards.t: Longitudinal, survey, quasi-experimental and field research
q: what is quasi-experimental research
what is the difference between experimental and quasi-experimental
what is field research
cards.x:
Research methods can also be sorted by how much control the researcher has over treatment and over who goes into which group.

- Longitudinal: measures and reports change over time (observational).
- Survey: gives an overview of the research question using purpose-built questions (observational).
- Policy research or evaluation: determines whether a program works or a policy is helpful (observational).
- Experimental: the researcher controls both the treatment and the assignment to groups.
- Quasi-experimental: the researcher controls the treatment but not the assignment, so there is less control. It sits between observational and experimental.
- Field research: common in epidemiology during investigations, such as new screening tests and vaccine trials. It can be either observational or experimental.

cards.t: The goal of research design and the usual study sequence
q: what is the goal of epidemiologic and clinical research
why does temporal sequence matter
what order do study designs come in
cards.x:
The goal of research is an unbiased comparison between a group with a factor and a group without it. Good design lets you compare two or more groups, quantify the risk difference, determine temporal sequence (which came first) and minimize biases. Temporal sequence bears on causation.

A cohort study starting from exposure establishes it most directly, because the exposure is recorded before the outcome occurs. A cross-sectional design measures both at the same moment, so it cannot say which came first. It is used for generating hypotheses.

Evidence usually builds in a sequence: clinical observations, available data, case-control studies, cohort studies, then randomized trials. Another way to see it: ideas become hypotheses, then observational studies, then experimental studies, and finally evidence-based information.

cards.t: Cross-sectional, ecologic and longitudinal ecologic studies
q: what is a cross-sectional study
what is an ecologic study
what is the difference between a cross-sectional survey and an ecologic study
cards.x:
A cross-sectional study is observational and used for generating hypotheses. It looks at one point in time.

- Cross-sectional survey: risk factor and disease are measured at the same time, using individual-level data. Examples: obesity in a population at one point, colorectal cancer screening by fecal occult blood testing, and varicella titers showing what share of a population is immune.
- Cross-sectional ecologic study: uses population-level data, relating how common a trait is to an outcome across populations rather than within individuals. Example: during the 1996 Atlanta Olympics, streets were blocked off, car emissions fell, and emergency visits for childhood asthma fell.
- Longitudinal ecologic survey: ongoing surveillance or repeated surveys that measure trends, such as whether lung cancer incidence rises as smoking rises among women.

cards.t: The ecologic fallacy
q: what is the ecologic fallacy
why can't I apply population data to one patient
cards.x:
The ecologic fallacy is applying aggregate data to an individual. Ecologic studies use population-level data. So what is true of a whole group's averages is not necessarily true of any one person inside it.

It is the standing hazard of population-level data. For example, if emergency visits for asthma fell across a city when traffic emissions fell, that tells you about the population. It does not tell you that any particular child's asthma was caused by traffic.

cards.t: Case-control versus cohort studies
q: what is the difference between a case-control and a cohort study
how are case-control groups chosen
what must a cohort study do well
cards.x:
The two designs are mirror images, and the difference is how people are grouped.

Case-control: groups are defined by outcome (disease or no disease), then assessed for differences in exposure or risk factors. It looks backward, from outcome to cause. It is observational and can generate or test hypotheses.

Cohort: a cohort is a group of people with a common trait, assembled at a similar point and followed over time. The trait can be age, date of birth, exposure to a risk factor, occupation, having a specific disease, or taking part in an intervention. Groups are formed by exposure, not outcome, and it looks forward from exposure to outcome. It is observational and used for testing hypotheses.

A good cohort needs a comparison group as similar as possible except for the exposure. It must be followed long enough for the outcome to appear, and completely, so that drop-outs do not falsely skew the results.

cards.t: What a randomized controlled trial needs
q: what is a randomized controlled trial
what are the requirements of a randomized controlled trial
why is a randomized controlled trial experimental
cards.x:
A randomized controlled trial is experimental and used for testing hypotheses. It is experimental because the investigator assigns and manipulates the intervention instead of watching an exposure that arose on its own.

Its ingredients: a clearly formed hypothesis and a study protocol; subjects randomly assigned to treatment and control; single or double blinding; an adequate sample size; and an account of withdrawals and drop-outs, since losing participants can distort the outcome. The results also have to be applicable to a larger population, because a finding confined to the sample cannot guide practice. That is external validity.

cards.t: Rates and the common mortality rates
q: what is a rate
how is infant mortality rate calculated
what is the difference between neonatal and postneonatal mortality
cards.x:
A rate is the number of times an event occurs during a fixed time period. Rates exist because they allow comparison, which a raw count cannot. A raw count, such as 800,000 deaths in a year, is not a rate because it has no denominator.

- Crude death rate: all deaths in the interval over the mid-interval population, per 1,000 or 100,000.
- Cause-specific death rate: deaths from one cause over the mid-interval population, per 100,000.
- Death-to-case ratio: deaths from a cause over new cases of the same disease, times 100.
- Neonatal mortality: deaths under 28 days per 1,000 live births. Postneonatal: deaths at 28 to 364 days. Infant mortality: deaths under 1 year, also per 1,000 live births, and it is commonly used to compare health status between nations.
- Maternal mortality: pregnancy-related deaths per 100,000 live births.

Incidence and prevalence are the morbidity rates, which concern illness in the living.

cards.t: Proportionate mortality (why it is not a true rate)
k: percent of deaths from a cause
q: what is proportionate mortality
why is proportionate mortality not a rate
why do proportionate mortality figures add to 100 percent
cards.x:
Proportionate mortality is the deaths from one specific cause divided by the total deaths from all causes, expressed per 100 or 1,000. In other words, it tells you what share of all deaths a cause accounts for.

It is not a rate, because its denominator is deaths rather than population. Since every cause is a share of the same total, the causes must sum to 100%.

cards.t: Age-adjusted rates, case fatality and years of potential life lost
q: why use an age-adjusted rate
what is case fatality
what is years of potential life lost
cards.x:
An age-adjusted rate removes the effect of a population's age structure. That makes it the right measure for comparing a county with its state: on crude rates alone, a county with an older population would look less healthy. In 2009 the United States crude death rate was about 794 per 100,000, which corresponded to an age-adjusted rate of 741.

Age-specific mortality is limited to one particular age group.

Case fatality is a measure of disease severity: the proportion of those diagnosed who die from it.

Years of potential life lost counts the productive years a death takes away, so dying younger costs more. It is used to target interventions.

cards.t: Incidence versus prevalence
q: what is the difference between incidence and prevalence
how do I calculate prevalence and incidence
what study design measures prevalence
cards.x:
Prevalence is the portion of a group that has a condition at a point in time, a snapshot. Incidence is the portion who develop the condition during a period: new cases in previously healthy people.

Prevalence is measured by counting those with and without the condition, and surveys are useful. A prevalence study is a cross-sectional study, good for generating hypotheses and planning services, relatively inexpensive, but poor for showing cause and effect. Incidence is measured by following a population over time, so an incidence study is a cohort study. Point prevalence looks at each person at a single point in time, which need not be the same date for everyone; period prevalence counts cases present during a time period.

Worked example, a town of 1,000. In 2015, 80 have Disease X, so prevalence is 80/1000 = 8%. Between 2016 and 2018, 20 previously healthy people develop it. Incidence is 20/1000 = 2%, and 2018 prevalence is 100/1000 = 10%.

cards.t: Cumulative incidence versus incidence density (person-time)
q: what is incidence density
what are person-years
when do I use incidence density instead of cumulative incidence
cards.x:
Cumulative incidence is for a group of fixed size: new cases divided by the people you started with. Incidence density is for a changing (dynamic) population, where people move in and out. It is often used in clinical trials.

Its denominator is person-time instead of people. One person followed for 10 years contributes 10 person-years, so everyone adds as much time as they were actually watched. Error can arise from variation in how long people were followed.

cards.t: How incidence, prevalence and duration relate, and why prevalence matters
q: is incidence or prevalence bigger
how do I get average duration from prevalence and incidence
why does prevalence matter clinically
cards.x:
Which is bigger depends on how long the condition lasts. In a chronic disease, new patients keep being added to an existing group that does not shrink, so incidence is usually lower than prevalence. In an acute illness such as the common cold, people recover, so many are affected over a period while few are ill at any one moment. Prevalence may then be lower than incidence.

When incidence and prevalence are stable, average duration of disease equals prevalence divided by incidence. A prevalence of 1.5% with an incidence of 50 per 100,000 per year gives 30 years.

Prevalence matters clinically for two reasons: it prioritizes the differential (horses, not zebras), and it sets the pretest probability, which changes how a test result should be read.

cards.t: Case definition and population at risk
k: what influences measurement of disease frequency
q: how does the case definition change measured disease frequency
what is the population at risk
cards.x:
Most clinical information lies on a continuum rather than in two boxes of sick and well. So where you draw the line between case and non-case has a marked effect on how much disease you find. Case definition and detection efforts change the observed frequency of disease, whereas a larger sample only reduces random error and does not systematically raise the number.

The population at risk should include only people who are susceptible. Men, for example, are not included in a study of ovarian cancer. Limiting the population this way may curtail generalizability.

cards.t: Random, probability, convenience and grab samples
q: what is the difference between a random sample and a probability sample
what is a convenience sample
why use a probability sample
cards.x:
Sampling methods differ in how people end up in the study.

- Random: every individual has an equal chance of selection.
- Probability: each person has a known probability of selection, which may or may not be equal. This is useful when you need to investigate subgroups such as age or ethnicity, because a random sample of everyone might not deliver enough of a small subgroup. It represents the population only if enough people are sampled.
- Convenience: non-random, chosen because it is easy to reach, such as enrolling whoever happens to be available on the ward. A fixed rule such as every 10th admitted patient is often given as a convenience example in teaching, though strictly it is systematic sampling. Because selection is not by chance, it may misrepresent the population.
- Grab: researchers take whoever they can find, so availability decides who is in.

cards.t: Distribution of disease by person, place and time (endemic, epidemic, pandemic)
q: what is the difference between endemic, epidemic and pandemic
what does person place and time mean in epidemiology
cards.x:
Epidemiologists describe how a disease is distributed by person, place and time, and looking for patterns across those three is a large part of the job.

- Person: the profile of those affected, including behavior as well as demographics. Where do they eat and shop, what products do they use, what water do they drink, did they attend the same event?
- Place: endemic disease is limited by geographic location. Coccidioidomycosis, for example, is found mainly in the deserts of the southwestern United States and Mexico.
- Time: an epidemic is a concentration of new cases in a given time. A pandemic is widespread, and can spread rapidly (influenza, early 1900s) or slowly (HIV/AIDS).

Awareness matters too. Once people know about an epidemic, new cases are easier to diagnose, so measured frequency can rise partly because clinicians started looking.

cards.t: Disease surveillance: what it does and how cases are found
q: what is disease surveillance
why does surveillance need a baseline
what are the functions of surveillance
cards.x:
Surveillance is ongoing tracking of disease. It can be active or passive, and it operates at the national, state and county level. It helps establish a baseline, and without one you cannot recognize a rise in cases.

Its functions are to determine the magnitude of a health problem, understand a disease's natural history, and evaluate control strategies. It also detects outbreaks and epidemics (foodborne gastrointestinal disease, or Vibrio after Hurricane Katrina's floods). It documents geographic distribution and spread (tuberculosis on an international flight). It allows hypothesis testing about etiology through case-control or cohort studies. And it monitors changes in an infectious agent, such as emerging antibiotic resistance.

Cases are found through screening high-risk people (influenza in a nursing home resident, a restaurant worker with hepatitis A). They are also found through clinical syndromes, mortality (some cases are detected only at death), provider reporting of illness and laboratory reporting of positive results. Provider reporting allows tracking of contacts and exposures.

cards.t: Steps in investigating an outbreak
q: what are the steps of an outbreak investigation
what do you do first when you suspect an outbreak
why confirm that an epidemic really exists
cards.x:
An outbreak investigation starts by asking whether the situation is epidemic or endemic and working out the attack rate. Next, establish the diagnosis and a case definition, and confirm that an epidemic truly exists. An apparent rise may reflect better detection rather than more disease. That is why a baseline and a settled case definition come first. Then characterize cases by time, place and person. That includes the type of exposure, the route of spread and the timing of exposure.

After that: build an epidemic curve, develop hypotheses about source, type and route of spread, test them, and start control measures. The overall arc is: detect a possible outbreak, find cases, generate hypotheses, test them, solve the original source, control the outbreak, and decide it is over.

A case-control study compares exposures in ill and well people. It is especially useful for identifying how the disease is spread, which lets you control the outbreak and trace the source.

cards.t: The epidemic curve
q: what is an epi curve
what does an epidemic curve show
cards.x:
An epidemic curve is the number of cases plotted against time, usually by date of onset. It shows when an outbreak started and how it unfolded, which helps in forming hypotheses about the source.

The classic example is Legionnaires' disease in Philadelphia, plotted by date of onset from 1 July to 18 August 1976, following an American Legion convention. The curve ties the epidemic to a single gathering.

cards.t: Levels of measurement: nominal, ordinal, interval
q: what are the levels of measurement
what is the difference between nominal and ordinal
what is the difference between continuous and discrete data
cards.x:
The level of measurement decides what you can legitimately say about two values.

- Nominal: categories with no specified order, such as eye color. Nominal data can only be counted. A dichotomous variable is nominal with just two categories, like yes/no or present/absent.
- Ordinal: there is some order, but no defined intervals between categories. You can say one is more, less or equally desirable, but not by how much. Examples: cancer stage I to IV and pitting edema 1+ to 4+.
- Interval: order with defined, equal intervals, so you can say how much two values differ. Continuous interval data can take any value along a continuum, limited by the precision of measurement (blood pressure, weight). Discrete data takes only specific values (number of children, number of heart attacks).

cards.t: Validity versus reliability
q: what is the difference between validity and reliability
can a measurement be reliable but not valid
why is high reliability with low validity dangerous
cards.x:
Validity is the degree to which data measure what they are supposed to measure. Reliability is consistency: repeated attempts give similar results. It is also called reproducibility, repeatability or precision.

Validity is ensured by calibrating devices and comparing results with known values, and for subjective measures by using structured questions such as pain scales.

Picture a target. High validity and high reliability is a tight cluster on the bullseye. High validity and low reliability is a wide scatter centered on the truth. Low validity and low reliability is a wide scatter off target. The dangerous one is low validity with high reliability: a tight cluster in the wrong place. A measurement can be consistently wrong, and the agreement looks like confirmation when nothing is checked against a known standard.

cards.t: Content, criterion and construct validity
q: what is construct validity
what is the difference between content and criterion validity
cards.x:
These are three ways to judge validity when you can't physically verify a measurement.

- Content validity: does the measure include all dimensions of the relevant information and exclude the irrelevant? For depression, are the questions representative of accepted symptoms, such as feeling sad or blue for more than 2 weeks, irritability and difficulty sleeping?
- Criterion validity: do the measurements predict, or associate with, an observable response or event? Does a high scorer have the affect of a clinically depressed person? Does chronically high cholesterol come with xanthelasma?
- Construct validity: does the measure relate to other measures believed to be part of the same phenomenon? Would a clinician interviewing the patient reach the same determination as the screening test?

cards.t: Intrasubject, intraobserver and interobserver variation
q: what is the difference between intraobserver and interobserver variation
why do repeated measurements vary
what causes variation within one patient
cards.x:
Measurements fluctuate for two combined reasons: true biologic differences and variation in how we measure.

- Intrasubject: within one person. Blood pressure varies with biological variation, time of day, position and stress.
- Intraobserver: one observer on two occasions, like a radiologist reading the same radiograph differently at two times.
- Interobserver: two observers, as when one clinician grades a murmur 3 and another grades it 4.

Variation within one patient may be true biologic variation, measurement error, or biologic change that represents disease. Working out which it is matters, because intervention should be considered only for a true pathological change. Variation between patients can come from inherent biological differences, systematic differences in measurement conditions, or measurement error.

cards.t: Random versus systematic variation and measurement error
q: what is the difference between random and systematic error
why doesn't averaging fix systematic error
how does measurement error relate to reliability and validity
cards.x:
Variation in a measurement is either random or systematic, and the difference decides whether averaging can help.

True biologic variation is the sum of many unknown factors, each adding a small random effect, so consecutive systolic pressures under the same conditions will not be identical. Systematic variation happens when the conditions of measurement are known to affect the values, such as time of day, after a cigarette, patient position or the white coat phenomenon.

For measurement error:
- Random error is due to chance and is equally likely to fall above or below the true value. It means a lack of reliability. It balances out, so there is no net misrepresentation of the true state, though individual measurements can still mislead. Reduce it by taking an average and estimate it in the statistical analysis.
- Systematic error is a flaw in the process, such as staff logging abnormal fetal heart rates as more normal. It means a lack of validity and it biases results, and averaging does not help.

cards.t: Mean, median, mode, range and standard deviation
q: what is the difference between mean median and mode
what is the interquartile range
what does standard deviation measure
cards.x:
A frequency distribution shows how many people, or what proportion, have each value. It is described by central tendency (the middle) and dispersion (the spread). It can be used on nominal and interval data, more commonly interval in clinical studies.

Central tendency:
- Mean: the sum of all values divided by the number of observations. It is the best estimate of central tendency, but extreme outliers can pull it.
- Median: the middle score, with half above and half below.
- Mode: the most frequently occurring value.

Dispersion:
- Range: all values from lowest to highest.
- Interquartile range: a limited range, such as the data between the 25th and 75th percentiles.
- Standard deviation: the variability of the scores about the mean.

cards.t: The normal (Gaussian) distribution and skewed distributions
q: what is the normal distribution
what percent of values fall within 1 and 2 standard deviations
what happens to the mean, median and mode when data are skewed
cards.x:
The normal distribution (also Gaussian or bell curve) is symmetric, with mean, median and mode coinciding. About two thirds of values fall within 1 standard deviation of the mean, and 95% within 2.

It is a mathematical model, based on theory and not on actual measurement. Naturally occurring clinical measurements may or may not resemble it.

When data are skewed, the three averages separate. In a right-skewed distribution, with a long right tail, extreme high values pull the mean toward the tail. So the mode is smallest, the median is in the middle and the mean is largest.

cards.t: Normal versus abnormal: defining abnormality
q: how is abnormal defined in medicine
does an abnormal result mean the patient is sick
why repeat an abnormal test
cards.x:
There is no clear-cut point at which disease begins. Disease is often acquired by degrees. It runs from susceptibility to a pre-symptomatic stage, then clinical disease, dysfunction and death.

So statistical abnormality does not necessarily mean clinical abnormality. A serum cholesterol of 201 is above the desired level but not clinically significant in itself, though risk is higher at high-normal than at low-normal. You can have an abnormal finding and not be sick, like a carrier of sickle cell trait. Some extremes are desirable: the lower end of the systolic blood pressure range, or the higher end of the high-density lipoprotein range. And a normal test does not necessarily rule out disease.

Abnormal should be defined by values known to be associated with disease, disability or death, or by a clinically recognizable difference from healthy. It should not be defined by whether values fit a normal curve. Abnormal tests should be confirmed by repeating them, because of regression to the mean: an extreme first result tends to come back closer to the usual value on repeat. Cutoffs are often arbitrary, so be careful of labeling.

cards.t: Before ordering a test: horses not zebras, and when to order
q: what does horses not zebras mean
when should I order a diagnostic test
what is the difference between a diagnostic test and a screening test
cards.x:
Start with the odds. Common diseases occur commonly, so when you hear hoofbeats think horses, not zebras. Uncommon presentations of common disease occur more often than common presentations of uncommon disease. But no disease is rare to the patient who has it.

Before ordering a test, weigh the risk against the benefit, know the test's limits, and consider cost. Avoid ordering tests indiscriminately and avoid repeating a test without an indication.

Diagnostic tests are for people with symptoms, and screening tests are for people without them. No test is absolutely accurate, but accuracy changes the probability of finding disease present or absent. So the quality of a test has to be assessed before you decide how to use and interpret it.

cards.t: The gold standard test
q: what is a gold standard test
why not always use the gold standard
how are new tests judged
cards.x:
A gold standard is any diagnostic procedure believed to identify the disease with certainty. Examples: culture for streptococcal throat infection, biopsy for cancer, cardiac catheterization for coronary artery disease, and endoscopy for peptic ulcer disease.

The catch is that gold standards are often expensive, invasive or risky, may not be acceptable to patients, and may not be easy to complete. So an alternative test is often the first choice, and the alternative is judged by how well it compares with the gold standard.

cards.t: The 2x2 table: sensitivity and specificity
q: how do I calculate sensitivity and specificity
what is the 2x2 table for a diagnostic test
what is the difference between sensitivity and specificity
cards.x:
The 2x2 table compares a new test with the gold standard. The columns are disease present or absent. The rows are test positive or negative. That gives four cells: true positives (a), false positives (b), false negatives (c) and true negatives (d).

- Sensitivity: the probability that a person with the disease has a positive result. True positives divided by everyone with disease, a / (a + c).
- Specificity: the probability that a person without the disease has a negative result. True negatives divided by everyone without disease, d / (b + d).

Both are calculated down the disease columns, so they are fairly fixed features of the test. Together they measure a test's validity, its ability to determine correctly who has the disease. Reliability is different: getting a similar result when the test is repeated under the same conditions.

cards.t: Positive and negative predictive value
q: what is positive predictive value
how do I calculate negative predictive value
why do predictive values depend on prevalence
cards.x:
Predictive values answer the question a patient actually asks: given my result, what are the chances I have the disease?

- Positive predictive value: the probability that a person with a positive result has the disease. True positives divided by all positives, a / (a + b).
- Negative predictive value: the probability that a person with a negative result is disease free. True negatives divided by all negatives, d / (c + d).

These are calculated across the test-result rows, so each one mixes the diseased and non-diseased columns, and that is why they depend on prevalence. Example with facial pain as a test for sinusitis: 49 of 128 positives have it, a positive predictive value of 38%, and 73 of 119 negatives are free of it, a negative predictive value of 61%.

In short, sensitivity and specificity guide which test to choose, while predictive values tell you what a given result means.

cards.t: Prevalence in the 2x2 table
q: how do I calculate prevalence from a 2x2 table
why does prevalence matter when interpreting tests
cards.x:
Prevalence is the proportion of the studied population that has the disease, which in the table is (a + c) divided by all four cells: everyone with the disease over everyone tested. The test result does not change it. In one study, 95 patients with sinusitis out of 247 gives a prevalence of 38%.

It is also the pretest probability in the population of interest. That matters twice. It prioritizes the differential diagnosis (think horses, not zebras), and it affects how test results should be interpreted, because it sets the pretest probability.

cards.t: Worked example: why a low-prevalence disease gives many false positives
q: why do false positives outnumber true positives in the ulcer example
how do I fill in a 2x2 table from numbers
cards.x:
In this example, 10,000 patients had both a new test and the gold standard, endoscopy, for peptic ulcer disease. Endoscopy found 25 ulcers, and the new test caught 20 of them (20 true positives, 5 false negatives). The new test also suggested an ulcer in 80 people whose endoscopy was negative (80 false positives, 9,895 true negatives).

Sensitivity is 20/25 = 80%. Specificity is 9,895/9,975 = 99%. Prevalence is only 25/10,000 = 0.25%.

The lesson is that even a 99% specific test throws up 80 false positives, because the pool of healthy people is so huge. With so few real cases, the 80 false positives outnumber the 20 true positives, which wrecks the positive predictive value.

cards.t: SnOUT and SpIN
q: what does SnOUT mean
what does SpIN mean
when do I want a highly sensitive test versus a highly specific one
cards.x:
These two rules tell you what a result can do for you.

- SnOUT: a negative result on a highly sensitive test rules disease out. High sensitivity means very few false negatives, so a negative is trustworthy. Use it when missing the disease has serious consequences.
- SpIN: a positive result on a highly specific test rules disease in. High specificity means very few false positives, so a positive is trustworthy. Use it when false positives would lead to unnecessary, risky or expensive work-ups.

A screening strategy follows from this: screen with a highly sensitive test, then confirm with a highly specific one.

Quick tip: sensitive tests are best at ruling out; specific tests are best at ruling in.

cards.t: Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve and the trade-off
q: what is an ROC curve
how do I tell which test is better from an ROC curve
are sensitivity and specificity related
cards.x:
A curve that plots the true positive rate against the false positive rate (which is 1 minus specificity) displays the whole sensitivity-specificity trade-off instead of one pair of values. The trade-off exists because sensitivity and specificity are inversely related: pushing one up usually pulls the other down, though ideally you maximize both.

The curve lets clinicians compare alternative tests for the same diagnosis. The better test's curve lies closest to the upper left corner and has the greatest area beneath it. It also helps decide where to set the cutoff point.

cards.t: Why predictive values change with prevalence
q: why does positive predictive value drop when prevalence is low
does prevalence change sensitivity and specificity
how does prevalence affect negative predictive value
cards.x:
Predictive values change with prevalence even when the test itself does not change. The numbers that matter in the exam room are the positive and negative predictive values: if the positive predictive value is 85%, a patient with a positive result has an 85% chance of really having the disease.

Take a test with 99% sensitivity and 95% specificity. At 1% prevalence, a positive result means only a 17% chance of disease (99/594). At 5% prevalence, the same positive result means 51% (495/970). Sensitivity and specificity were identical in both rows.

The direction is simple: as prevalence falls, positive predictive value falls and negative predictive value rises. As prevalence rises, positive predictive value rises and negative predictive value falls. The reason is that predictive values mix the diseased and healthy columns. When disease is uncommon, the healthy pool is so much larger that even a small false positive rate produces many false positives compared with the few true cases.

cards.t: Pretest and posttest probability
q: what is pretest probability
what is posttest probability
how does a test change the probability of disease
cards.x:
Pretest probability is the chance the patient has the disease based on what you know before the test. It is often simply the prevalence in the population the patient comes from. Posttest probability is the chance after the test result is in, and it is the number that informs treatment decisions.

The posttest probability is the pretest probability updated by the likelihood ratio, a number that says how strongly a test result shifts the probability. If a test has a likelihood ratio of about 1.0, as facial pain does for sinusitis, it changes nothing: the probability stays at 38%, equal to the prevalence and to the positive predictive value.

cards.t: Likelihood ratios: what they are and how to calculate them
q: what is a likelihood ratio
how do I calculate a positive likelihood ratio
do likelihood ratios depend on prevalence
cards.x:
A likelihood ratio tells you how much the probability that a patient has a condition changes once the test result is known. Unlike predictive values, it is not affected by prevalence.

- Positive likelihood ratio = sensitivity / (1 - specificity). It says how much more likely the condition is after a positive result. A ratio of 4 means the odds of the condition are 4 times what they were before the test.
- Negative likelihood ratio = (1 - sensitivity) / specificity. It says how much less likely the condition is after a negative result. A ratio of 0.5 means the odds of the condition are cut in half.

A ratio above 1 raises the posttest probability above the pretest, and a ratio below 1 lowers it. The ratio is a multiplier, not a probability. Strictly, it multiplies the odds of disease rather than the probability, which is why the odds method converts probability to odds first. Even a high-ratio test can mislead if the disease has a low prevalence.

cards.t: How big a likelihood ratio matters (the rule-of-thumb table)
k: rule in rule out likelihood ratio
q: what likelihood ratio is strong evidence to rule in
what does a likelihood ratio of 0.1 mean
what is an indeterminate likelihood ratio
cards.x:
As a rule of thumb, bigger distance from 1 means a bigger shift in probability. The approximate change in probability for the benchmark ratios:

- Above 10: strong evidence to rule in (a ratio of 10 adds about 45 percentage points).
- 5 to 10: moderate evidence to rule in (5 adds about 30).
- 0.5 to 2: indeterminate (2 adds about 15), so the test barely moves you.
- 0.2 to 0.5: weak evidence to rule out (0.5 subtracts about 15).
- 0.1 to 0.2: moderate evidence to rule out (0.2 subtracts about 30).
- Below 0.1: strong evidence to rule out (0.1 subtracts about 45).

A very low ratio, below about 0.1, virtually rules the disease out. When pretest probability is 30 to 70%, a very high ratio, above about 10, rules disease in. The shift is added to the starting point, so the pretest probability still matters.

cards.t: Getting posttest probability from a likelihood ratio (odds method and nomogram)
q: how do I calculate posttest probability using a likelihood ratio
how do I use the likelihood ratio nomogram
cards.x:
There are two ways to turn a pretest probability and a likelihood ratio into a posttest probability.

Math: convert the pretest probability to pretest odds, multiply by the likelihood ratio to get posttest odds, then convert back to a probability (odds divided by 1 plus odds).

Nomogram: find the pretest probability in the left column and the likelihood ratio in the center, and draw a straight line through both. The posttest probability is where the line crosses the right-hand column.

Worked numbers from a 38% pretest probability (pretest odds 0.61). When clinicians label a patient "high probability", that impression carries a likelihood ratio of 4.7, giving posttest odds of about 2.9, so about 74%. A "low probability" impression has a ratio of 0.4, giving odds of 0.24, so about 20%. An intermediate impression with a ratio of 1.4 is indeterminate and moves 38% only to about 46%.

cards.t: Worked example: rapid strep test likelihood ratios
q: how do I calculate likelihood ratios for the rapid strep test
what does a negative rapid strep test mean
cards.x:
A child with a fever, tender front neck nodes and tonsillar exudate (pus on the tonsils) has a rapid strep antigen test with sensitivity of 65% and specificity of 96%. Throat culture is the gold standard but takes 24 to 48 hours.

Step 1, the pretest probability comes from the modified Centor score: one point each for temperature above 38 degrees Celsius, absence of cough, tender anterior cervical nodes and tonsillar swelling or exudate, with an age adjustment.

Step 2, calculate the ratios. Positive ratio = 0.65 / (1 - 0.96) = 0.65 / 0.04 = 16.25, so a positive result multiplies the odds of strep by about 16. Negative ratio = (1 - 0.65) / 0.96 = 0.35 / 0.96 = 0.36, so a negative result cuts the odds of strep to about a third.

Step 3, read the posttest probability off the nomogram using the pretest probability from step 1. By the rule-of-thumb bands, a positive ratio above 10 is strong evidence to rule strep in, while 0.36 falls in the 0.2 to 0.5 band, only weak evidence to rule it out.

cards.t: Using multiple tests: parallel versus serial testing
q: what is the difference between serial and parallel testing
what does serial testing do to sensitivity and specificity
when should I use tests in series
cards.x:
Using multiple tests means running them in parallel (all at once) or in serial (one after another), and the choice pushes sensitivity and specificity in opposite directions. If the tests all agree, interpretation is easy. If they disagree, consider how they were done.

- Parallel (all at once): used when rapid diagnosis is preferred. Sensitivity and negative predictive value go up, so disease is less likely to be missed, but specificity and positive predictive value go down. How much sensitivity you gain depends on how well the tests complement each other, with one catching cases the other misses.
- Serial (one after another, each requires the previous to be positive): used when speed matters less, tests are expensive or risky, or after simpler and safer tests are inconclusive. Specificity and positive predictive value go up (fewer false positives), but sensitivity and negative predictive value go down. It uses fewer tests but takes more time.

Each test should contribute independent information, or combining them adds little. Example: an exercise tolerance test for coronary artery disease, then cardiac catheterization if it is positive.

cards.t: Questions to ask when appraising a new diagnostic test
q: how do I critically appraise a study of a new test
why should test readers be blinded
why check whether prevalence matches my patients
cards.x:
When you read a study of a new test, ask:

- What is the disease of interest, and what is the new test?
- Did the study include a spectrum of patients, meaning a range of patients rather than one narrow type?
- Did every subject get both the new test and the gold standard?
- Were the people doing each test blinded (kept unaware) of the other's result? One result could influence the reading of the other, which is a form of measurement bias.
- Are the benefits and risks of the new test reasonable?
- What are the sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value and negative predictive value?
- Is the prevalence of disease similar in your own patient population? Predictive values differ if prevalence differs, so a published value may not transfer to your setting.

The diagnosis of disease is only as good as the tests used to measure it.

cards.t: What a risk factor is
q: what is a risk factor
does a risk factor guarantee disease
is a treatment that lowers risk a risk factor
cards.x:
A risk factor is a factor associated with an increase in the probability of developing a disease later. It raises the probability but does not make the disease certain, so risk factors describe groups of people, not a guaranteed outcome for one person.

Two things are not risk factors. A factor that is present only after the disease has begun is not one, because it did not come first. And a treatment that lowers the chance of disease is a protective intervention.

Example for congestive heart failure: smoking, hypertension, hypercholesterolemia, family history, diabetes and valvular disease.

cards.t: Why some risk factors are easy to spot and others are hidden
q: why are some risk factors hard to detect
how does long latency hide a risk factor
which design is better for a rare disease
cards.x:
Whether a risk factor is noticed depends on the pattern of exposure and disease.

- Easy: a large risk with rapid effects. A big effect soon after exposure is hard to miss, especially in a new disease with no established risk factors competing.
- Long latency between exposure and disease: the disease appears long after the exposure, so the two look unrelated unless people are followed long enough.
- Frequent exposure: it may be obscured unless exposed are compared with unexposed. When most people are exposed, the disease may seem ordinary.
- Low disease incidence: a small risk produces few extra cases, so a larger population is needed to see a difference.
- Common disease with known risk factors: it is hard to distinguish new ones.
- One risk factor can contribute to many outcomes.

Following a rare disease in a cohort requires a very large cohort, so a case-control study is better for rare disease.

cards.t: What risk is used for: prediction, cause, diagnosis, prevention
q: what are risk factors used for
does a risk factor prove causation
what is the best predictor of disease in an individual patient
cards.x:
Risk information serves four purposes.

- Prediction of a future event. The probabilities are based on groups, and relative risk is calculated to determine the probability.
- Cause. Risk factors may predict disease without causing it. A factor that predicts without causing is a disease marker, so prediction does not prove causation.
- Diagnosis. Risk factors increase the probability of getting the disease, but the best predictor in an individual is the presence of early clinical disease.
- Prevention. Removing a risk factor lowers the probability of developing the disease. Examples: controlling hypertension to prevent heart failure, avoiding second-hand smoke, and advising a patient to stop smoking. Another is controlling dietary intake to prevent obesity and so decrease the likelihood of type II diabetes mellitus.

cards.t: How risk is studied: why observational designs are used
q: why can't risk be studied with a randomized trial
which designs are used to study risk
cards.x:
Experimental studies of risk in humans are limited by ethics. Investigators cannot ethically assign people to a harmful exposure. So risk is studied with observational designs: a concurrent (prospective) cohort, a historical (retrospective) cohort, or a case-control study.

For example, randomly assigning people to heavy cell phone use is an ethical problem if it is potentially harmful. Also, people would not accept long-term restrictions on using their phones. So a trial of it is unlikely.

cards.t: Relative risk: calculating and reading it
q: what is relative risk
how do I interpret a relative risk of 2.5
what does a relative risk of 1 mean
what does a relative risk less than 1 mean
cards.x:
Relative risk asks how many times more likely exposed people are than unexposed people to get the disease. It is the incidence in the exposed divided by the incidence in the unexposed. It measures the strength of association between exposure and outcome. Raw case counts cannot be compared directly because the groups differ in size. So first turn each count into an incidence (cases divided by the people in the group), then divide the two.

- Equal to 1 is the null value: no association between exposure and disease.
- Above 1: risk is higher with the exposure. A relative risk of 2.5 means exposed persons are 2.5 times as likely to develop the disease. 1.25 is 25 percent higher, and 1.4 is 40 percent higher.
- Below 1: a negative association that may be protective, as with an effective vaccine. A relative risk of 0.6 means 40 percent lower risk. For prevention we expect it to be below 1.

It is a ratio, not a percentage, and it can never be negative.

cards.t: Worked example: birth control pills and thrombophlebitis
q: how do I calculate relative risk from a 2x2 table
why is the birth control pill example not a randomized trial
cards.x:
For 10 years, 2,000 women were followed: 1,000 randomly selected young women on birth control pills and 1,000 randomly selected nonusers. 30 pill users developed thrombophlebitis, compared with 3 nonusers.

Risk in users = 30/1,000 = 0.03. Risk in nonusers = 3/1,000 = 0.003. Relative risk = 0.03 / 0.003 = 10. So women on the pill are 10 times more likely to develop thrombophlebitis. Had the relative risk been 1, there would be no association.

Why isn't this a randomized controlled trial? The women were randomly selected but not randomly assigned to take the pill. Random assignment of the exposure is what defines a randomized trial, so this is a prospective cohort study. Following people forward in time is common to cohort studies and trials alike, and equal group sizes don't distinguish them.

cards.t: Predicting risk from groups: calibration and discrimination
k: risk estimate is a group probability
q: what is calibration in a risk model
what is discrimination in a risk model
what does a 2 percent risk of colorectal cancer mean for one patient
cards.x:
A risk prediction model is judged two ways, calibration and discrimination. Behind them is one idea: risk is a prediction about a future event, and the probabilities are based on groups of people, not on one patient followed in detail. A 2% chance of colorectal cancer in the next 5 years means the patient is a member of a group in which a very small number will develop it. For an individual patient, the best predictor is the presence of early clinical disease.

- Calibration: how well the predicted probability matches the observed proportion. If points lie consistently off the line of perfect agreement, predicted rates are consistently higher or lower than observed, so calibration is poor; which direction above the line means depends on which axis shows the predicted rate.
- Discrimination: how well it separates people who will develop the disease from those who will not. A model discriminates poorly when the estimated-risk curves of those who did and did not develop disease heavily overlap.

They are separate properties. A model can be well calibrated yet discriminate poorly, and it can still give useful risk estimates. Risk models can predict onset, diagnosis and prognosis.

cards.t: Absolute risk and incidence (and predicting cases from relative risk)
q: what is absolute risk
how do I calculate expected cases from a relative risk
which study design gives incidence directly
cards.x:
Absolute risk is the possibility of an event in the population under study, which is the incidence of disease in that population. It does not tell you whether exposure is associated with higher risk.

Incidence = new cases over a given time divided by the number of people in the group. It counts only new cases, and the denominator is people, not other cases. For example, 18 new cases among 600 people is 18 / 600 = 0.03, or 3 percent.

A cohort study establishes incidence directly, because it follows exposed and unexposed people forward and sees who develops disease. A case-control study starts from people who already have the condition, so it can't.

To predict cases: exposed incidence = relative risk x unexposed incidence, then multiply by the number of people. With an unexposed incidence of 0.05 and a relative risk of 3, the exposed incidence is 0.15, so 200 exposed people produce 0.15 x 200 = 30 cases.

cards.t: What a cohort is and how it must be followed
q: what is a cohort study of risk
why does cohort study follow-up need to be complete
is reviewing past charts a cohort study
cards.x:
A cohort is a group of people with a common trait, assembled at a similar point and followed over time. The trait may be age, date of birth, exposure to a risk factor, having a specific disease, or taking part in a preventive or therapeutic intervention.

In a cohort study of risk, people without disease are divided into those exposed to a risk factor and those not exposed. Both groups are followed to see what proportion of each develops disease, and relative risk can be calculated.

Two requirements: follow them long enough to observe the expected outcome, and follow them completely, so attrition (people dropping out) does not falsely skew the outcome data. A larger control group does not replace lost participants. Also check that the data points collected actually relate to the study.

Looking back at the course of patients already under care, with no common starting point, is not a cohort study.

cards.t: Prospective (concurrent) versus retrospective (historical) cohorts
q: what is the difference between prospective and retrospective cohorts
what is a retrospective cohort study
what are the weaknesses of historical and concurrent cohorts
is a case-control study retrospective
cards.x:
Both kinds of cohort group people by exposure and follow them forward. The difference is where the investigator stands in time.

- Historical (retrospective): the cohort is assembled in the past from records, with exposures determined at that historical point, then followed forward to the present, so the outcomes have already occurred.
